For starters, I'd suggest using prepared statements and bind_param() instead of inserting escaped text directly into the SQL text. Yes, it'll work but IIRC, prepared statements are more efficient.

Next, I'd suggest changing your code to print $_POST['Story'] directly onto the page, and (if you want to stay with your string-interpolation approach to the SQL statement) print out the SQL as well. The problem is that you're purifying $Story into $clean_html, but then when you escape it, you're escaping the original $_POST['Story'] rather than escaping your purified $clean_html. So instead of this at line 86:

$clean_html = $purifier->purify($Story);
$clean_html = mysqli_real_escape_string($conn, $_POST['Story']);

you want this:

$Story = $purifier->purify($_POST['Story']);
$clean_html = mysqli_real_escape_string($conn, $Story);

It is time to end prosecutorial immunity.

Let me give a counterpoint from my experience as a lawyer (to be clear never as a prosecutor):

  1. In my experience, a very good way to make an allegation against you lose steam is to make some allegations against the complainant. For example, if you haven't paid the $100,000 you owe to your accountants and they sue you for the unpaid money then its a convenient time to have a close look and see if you can allege that they were negligent.

  2. Not many people can afford to conduct litigation. Those who get pro bono representation are lucky but generally, running a civil case is expensive. Running a civil case is re-mortgage your house kind of expensive.

  3. Being sued is also expensive. Even if you win, you still spend thousands upon legal representation and you very very rarely recover 100% through a costs award. Just the threat of being sued is terrifying, even if you are 100% sure you did nothing wrong.

I have no difficulty envisioning a reality where well resourced defendants suggest to prosecutors that "when this case is all over, we'll be suing you for prosecutorial misconduct" in an attempt to gain leverage in settlement negotiations or to have charges withdrawn. As a prosecutor, why would you risk that? Why go after a high-profile defendant where losing means losing your house? Why not just prosecute people who don't have the financial resources to ruin your life in retaliation? Not that all prosecutors would do that but given the level of integrity among prosecutors we're already complaining about how likely do you think it is that you can have all prosecutors be truth-and-justice-at-any-costs-and-forget-about-my-personal-risk types?

Do you want to have an immunity which causes problems in some cases where prosecutors engage in misconduct or have no immunity and have that cause a problem in all cases because your prosecutors are gun shy?

I don't know the answer, but there are two sides to the coin.

@BigBadWolf Thank you for taking the time to post this. You make great points.

How would you propose dealing with prosecutorial misconduct? Shouldn't prosecutors, like everyone else, be accountable for their actions?

Like I said, I'm not sure what the answer is. If I had the answer I'd run for office or something.

Maybe removing the immunity for the state but not the individuals. If there is prosecutorial malfeasance then the state can compensate the victim but the prosecutor themselves bears no personal liability. If their misconduct starts taking six-figure chunks out of their department's budget to settle misconduct cases then bad prosecutors may quickly find themselves without a job.

A split-profession for prosecutors like we have in commonwealth countries might help but I don't know how you could work that in the US.
